title: Inventory optimization ROI for retail: build the case
summary: Inventory optimization ROI comes from lower carrying cost, fewer stockouts, and smaller markdowns. A worked case shows 128% ROI even at half the benefits.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 12 October 2026.


Inventory optimization ROI for retail is the yearly gain from three sources (lower carrying cost on stock you no longer hold, sales recovered from fewer stockouts, and smaller markdowns) minus the program cost, divided by that cost. The calculation is simple, and what finance will challenge is how each input was measured.


Priya, the supply chain director at a home goods retailer, took a business case to her CFO last spring. It leaned on a vendor's published benchmark of "up to 30% less inventory." The CFO asked one question: what does that mean for our products, our locations, our carrying cost? Nobody could answer it, and the project waited six months. (Priya is an illustrative example.) The second attempt used the retailer's own DIO, markdown ledger, and stockout counts, and it was approved in one meeting.


This guide shows how to build that second version. It covers the formula, how to measure each of the three levers, a worked example with real arithmetic, and the places where business cases usually break. If you would rather model it on your own assortment, you can[see what product-level optimization would change on your data](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


> **Key Takeaways**
>
>
> - Inventory optimization ROI has three recurring sources: carrying cost on stock you no longer hold, margin on sales recovered from fewer stockouts, and markdown cost avoided.
> - IHL Group puts retail inventory distortion, the combined cost of overstocks and out-of-stocks, at $1.73 trillion a year, or 6.5% of global retail sales (September 2025).
> - In the worked example below, a EUR60M retailer that cuts inventory 10%, recovers 20% of lost sales, and trims markdown cost 10% gains EUR684k a year against a EUR150k program: 356% ROI and a 2.6 month payback.
> - Halving every benefit in that example still returns 128% in year one with a 5.3 month payback, and the case breaks even at 22% of the base benefits.
> - McKinsey reports that early adopters of AI-enabled supply chain management cut inventory levels by 35%. Treat that as a ceiling for the leading group, and plan on a far smaller number.


## What is inventory optimization ROI?


Inventory optimization ROI is the net financial return from setting stock targets more precisely: (annual recurring benefit minus program cost) divided by program cost. Payback is the program cost divided by monthly benefit. A one-time cash release from lower inventory sits next to both figures, because it is working capital rather than profit.


Optimization here means deciding how much of each product to hold at each location and at what service level, using demand forecasts, lead times, margin, and holding cost. That covers safety stock, reorder points, order quantities, and allocation. If the distinction between this and day-to-day stock handling is new to you, our guide to inventory management vs inventory optimization draws the line.


The case rests on three benefits that you can measure from systems you already have. Each one maps to a line in the P&L or the balance sheet, and that mapping is what makes the number defensible.


## The three sources of return, and how to measure each


### Lower carrying cost on stock you no longer hold


Carrying cost is what it costs to own a euro of inventory for a year: cost of capital, storage and handling, shrinkage, insurance, and obsolescence. Take the percentage from your finance team, because the range differs a lot between a fast-moving beauty range and a slow jewelry assortment.


The calculation is the inventory reduction at cost times your carrying cost rate. Express the reduction in days too. DIO, days inventory outstanding, equals average inventory at cost divided by cost of goods sold, times 365. Finance already tracks it, and it translates a stock target directly into cash.


### Margin on sales recovered from fewer stockouts


A stockout costs the margin on the sale you did not make, plus some customers who do not come back. Measure lost sales from product-level data: days at zero stock on products with demand, multiplied by the sales rate those products had when in stock.


Count only the margin, not the revenue. A recovered euro of revenue is worth the gross margin percentage, so a team that reports revenue uplift will overstate the benefit and lose the finance review. Our article on[the hidden cost of inaccurate sales forecasts](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/the-hidden-cost-of-inaccurate-sales-forecasts) covers how forecast error turns into missed sales.


### Markdown cost avoided


Markdown cost is the value you give away to clear stock: original price minus sale price, times units sold at a discount. Your markdown ledger has it by product and season. Optimization acts here by buying and positioning less of what will not sell at full price, so fewer units end up on the clearance rail.


Take the markdown figure from the ledger as it is, then set a modest reduction. Better targets help most on products with a high markdown share, so start with the products that account for the largest part of markdown cost.


## A worked inventory optimization ROI example you can rebuild in a spreadsheet


The figures below describe an illustrative retailer, not a client. Every input is an assumption you should replace with your own.


The retailer has EUR60M in annual revenue and EUR36M in cost of goods sold. Average inventory at cost is EUR12M, which gives a DIO of 121.7 days (12 / 36 x 365). Finance says carrying cost is 25% of inventory value. About 3% of revenue (EUR1.8M) is lost to stockouts, gross margin is 40%, and markdown cost is EUR2.4M, or 4% of revenue.


The team assumes the program reduces inventory by 10%, recovers 20% of lost sales, and cuts markdown cost by 10%. Those are deliberately modest.


Benefit Calculation Annual value


Carrying cost saved EUR1.2M less inventory x 25% EUR300k


Margin from recovered sales EUR1.8M lost x 20% = EUR360k revenue x 40% margin EUR144k


Markdown cost avoided EUR2.4M x 10% EUR240k


**Total recurring benefit** **EUR684k**


One-time cash released EUR1.2M (DIO from 121.7 to 109.5 days) EUR1.2M


Assume the first-year program cost is EUR150k, covering software, integration, and team time. Use a real quote for this line, since the number here is a placeholder.


ROI in year one is (684 - 150) / 150, or 356%. Payback is 150 / 684 x 12, or 2.6 months. These are the numbers a vendor would put on a slide, and they are the ones finance will discount, so show the conservative version beside them.


Scenario Annual benefit ROI, year one Payback


Base case EUR684k 356% 2.6 months


Every benefit halved EUR342k 128% 5.3 months


Break-even EUR150k 0% 12 months


The break-even row answers a skeptical CFO directly: the program pays for itself if it delivers 22% of the base benefits. A sponsor who can say that sentence in a meeting has already answered the first objection.


## What belongs on the cost side


Counting only the software license flatters the case. Include integration work, data cleanup, and the planner time spent in the first two cycles. Add any change in service-level policy that could raise stock on some products, because optimization sometimes recommends more of a high-margin item than the old uniform rule held.


Ongoing costs matter as well: subscription, support, and a planner's weekly review time. Most of the planner time disappears if the team moves to exception-based review. The saved hours are real, yet they are rarely cash, so keep them in a note instead of the headline number.


## Where business cases break


Three mistakes account for most of the rejected cases we hear about.


**Counting the same euro twice.** Lower inventory and lower markdowns often come from the same decision, buying less of a slow product. If you claim the carrying cost saving on that stock and the markdown saving on the same units, you have counted one improvement in two columns. Assign each product's benefit to one lever, or net out the overlap.


**Assuming the benefit starts on day one.** Forecasts need a few cycles to settle, and inventory only falls as old stock sells through. A realistic model ramps benefits over two to three quarters. Our ROI example uses a full year for clarity, so apply your own ramp to the cash timing.


**Borrowing a headline result.** McKinsey's research on AI-enabled supply chain management reports that early adopters improved logistics costs by 15%, inventory levels by 35%, and service levels by 65% against slower-moving competitors. That describes the leading group in a large study. It is a sound reason to take the topic seriously and a poor input for your model, which should come from your own data.


Across Metreecs' work with specialty retailers, finance teams approve business cases fastest when the stockout and markdown inputs come from their own ledgers and each lever is assigned to a distinct set of products.


Marcus leads buying for a sporting goods retailer with 45 stores. His first draft claimed EUR500k in markdown savings and EUR400k in carrying cost savings on the same overstocked range of winter products. Finance spotted the overlap in ten minutes. After he split the products into two lists, one for markdown avoidance and one for stock reduction, the combined benefit dropped by about a third and the case was approved. (Marcus is an illustrative example with round numbers.)


## How to present the inventory optimization business case to finance


Build the case in a sequence that lets your finance partner check each step. The order below works for most teams.


1. Pull a baseline: average inventory at cost, COGS, DIO, markdown cost, and lost sales by product for the last 12 months.
2. Agree the carrying cost rate and the gross margin percentage with finance before you calculate anything.
3. Choose the products where the three levers are largest, and assign each one to a single lever.
4. Set the improvement assumptions low, and show a second scenario with every benefit halved.
5. List all costs, including integration and planner time, and state when the first benefits appear.
6. Define the measures you will track after launch, such as DIO, stockout rate, and markdown rate, with a review date.


Renewal and next-phase decisions get made on whether you hit the numbers you promised, so pick measures you can read monthly. Our guide to[KPIs for networked inventory](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/managing-networked-inventory-which-kpis-to-track-for-effective-control) explains how to read DIO, service level, and stockout rate together.


The scale of the problem supports the case without being its centerpiece. IHL Group's September 2025 analysis estimates inventory distortion at $1.73 trillion a year. Our piece on[moving from stockouts to overstock control with AI](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/from-stockouts-to-overstock-can-ai-be-the-balancing-solution) explains why both problems often sit in the same assortment.


Aiko plans inventory for a beauty brand with about 300 products. She presented the three-lever model with the halved scenario, then added a one-page monthly tracker. Six months after launch she reported DIO and stockout rate against the baseline, and the board approved a second phase covering more locations. (Aiko is an illustrative example.) The tracker, more than the original ROI figure, is what kept the project funded.


In our experience deploying product-level optimization, the retailers that sustain the gains are those that keep one owner for the baseline numbers, so the comparison stays honest as the assortment changes.


## Where AI-powered optimization changes the numbers


Spreadsheet-era optimization recalculated targets once or twice a year, because each pass took weeks. AI-powered[demand planning](https://www.metreecs.com/demand-planning) produces a product x location forecast with an uncertainty range, and[AI-driven inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) recalculates safety stock and reorder points from it every cycle.


That shifts the business case in two ways. Benefits show up faster, because targets keep adjusting as demand moves. And the effort to maintain the program falls, since planners review exceptions and leave routine decisions to the system. Leave both out of a first model and document them as upside.


## FAQ


### How do you calculate inventory optimization ROI?


Add the annual carrying cost saved, the gross margin on recovered sales, and the markdown cost avoided. Subtract the program cost and divide by that cost. Payback is the program cost divided by the monthly benefit.


### What is a good ROI for inventory optimization?


It depends on your starting point. A retailer with high DIO and heavy markdowns has more to recover than one already running lean. Rather than chase a benchmark, aim for a case that still pays back in under 12 months when every benefit is halved.


### How long does it take to see a return?


Stockout and markdown improvements usually appear within one or two planning cycles. Inventory falls more slowly, since existing stock has to sell through. Plan a ramp over two to three quarters and track DIO monthly.


### Which costs should I include?


Include software, integration, data cleanup, and the planner time spent in the first cycles, plus any rise in stock on high-margin products. Leave soft savings, such as hours freed, in a note instead of the headline figure.


### What data do I need to build the business case?


You need average inventory at cost, COGS, markdown cost by product, a measure of lost sales from stockouts, your carrying cost rate, and gross margin. A year of history by product and location is enough to start.


## Conclusion


Inventory optimization ROI for retail holds up when each lever comes from your own ledgers, each product is counted once, and a halved scenario still pays back. Build that version first, and the discussion with finance becomes about timing and tracking instead of whether the numbers are real.
